title: Does AI-Powered Clinical Documentation Enhance Clinician Efficiency? A Longitudinal Study
Rapid comparative evaluation of 2 ambient artificial intelligence applications in a learning health system.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To evaluate ambient Artificial Intelligence (AI) scribe systems (AAS) across multiple domains using a rapid learning health system (LHS) approach, including provider satisfaction, efficiency, documentation quality, usability, and patient sentiment. This LHS evaluation compared 2 AAS systems (Abridge and Nabla) among 100 providers over 90 days. Evaluation incorporated a cluster randomized crossover comparison, analysis of use and EHR-based workflow outcomes, and standardized simulated encounters to assess documentation quality and safety. Outcomes included provider satisfaction, efficiency, note quality, usability, and patient sentiment. In standardized simulated encounters, both systems achieved 76% note element accuracy with minimal risk for harm. In the randomized crossover comparison, Abridge demonstrated higher usability scores (78.5 vs 73) and was preferred 3:1 over Nabla, which had higher automated speech recognition error rates. Across 16 479 clinical encounters, AAS was used in 35.7% of visits. Total EHR time decreased by approximately 5 minutes per day; same-day chart closure increased by approximately 5% during the initial crossover period, but this effect was attenuated. Provider experience was positive (Net Promoter Score [NPS] 53). Both systems demonstrated comparable documentation accuracy and modest efficiency gains while improving clinician satisfaction. Despite similar performance, clinicians reported differences in usability and preference. Adoption below 40% reflected the trade-off between documentation support and verification burden. Rapid, multidimensional evaluation within a LHS can assess AAS across domains of implementation, efficiency, clinician experience, and documentation quality and safety. Ongoing monitoring of efficiency, documentation quality, and use patterns is essential.

title: Challenges in AI based tumor board case summarization and recommendations
desc: Tumor boards, recurring meetings at hospital institutions, assemble cancer specialists (e.g., medical oncology and pathology) to discuss patient care. In this work, we formally define tumor board case summarization, options generation, and meeting outcome prediction as AI tasks. We study datasets from four medical institutions and evaluate state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) from the DeepSeek, GPT, Gemini, and Qwen families using expert human assessment. Medical oncologists created ~9.6k reference texts and 16k human judgments across tasks. Clinicians rated LLM-generated case summaries 3.57–4.59 out of 5.0 across institutions, but recommendation generation remained more challenging, with average scores of 2.0–3.6. Clinical alignment analyses showed modest correlations of ~0.2 for case summarization subtasks and higher correlations of ~0.6 for recommendation generation using LLM-as-Judge metrics. Our proposed TBFact metrics were competitive with LLM-as-Judge approaches in longer prose free-text settings, suggesting a promising direction toward explainable evaluation. This study, to our knowledge the largest expert-grading study of tumor board tasks with both granular and direct assessments, found that criterion-level scores and overall judgments are related nonlinearly. Experts also frequently assigned high ratings to responses that differed substantially from their reference texts, challenging assumptions underlying reference-based automatic evaluation metrics.

title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Shaping the future of venous thromboembolism diagnosis and prognosis.
desc: [Artificial intelligence in medicine] Venous thromboembolism (VTE) continues to pose a substantial health issue worldwide, characterized by high rates of mortality and morbidity. The field of artificial intelligence (AI) has shown potential as a valuable asset for enhancing the detection and prediction of complex diseases, such as VTE. This review explores the role of AI in VTE prediction and diagnosis, analyzing various machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches, including natural language processing (NLP), support vector machines (SVM), random forests (RF), logistic regression (LR), gradient boosting methods, and deep learning frameworks such as ClotCatcher. Among the artificial intelligence models, those based on natural language processing algorithms, particularly ClotCatcher, demonstrated strong performance in analyzing unstructured clinical data. ClotCatcher achieved exceptional Area under the Curve (AUC) values of 0.980 and 0.995 for venous thromboembolism (VTE) adjudication from radiology reports. AI-driven methodologies facilitate early detection, personalized risk assessment, and enhanced patient outcomes. AI holds great potential for improving VTE diagnosis and risk assessment, offering greater accuracy and efficiency than traditional methods. However, further studies are required to validate these models across diverse populations and clinical environments. The integration of AI in VTE management represents a promising frontier in personalized medicine, potentially leading to improved outcomes and more efficient healthcare delivery.

title: Evaluating the Feasibility of an Artificial-Intelligence Based Clinical Decision Support Tool for People With Chronic Lung Disease
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University of Pennsylvania; conditions: Population Health Management, Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS), Chronic Lung Diseases, Artificial Intelligence (AI); type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 45; status: RECRUITING] Patients living with chronic lung diseases (CLD) are at high risk of frailty, malnutrition, and depression. However, many of the interventions targeting these conditions are underutilized. Thus, artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) offer a promising approach to guide targeted interventions for this population and reduce risk of hospitalization. The purpose of this study is to assess the acceptability and feasibility of a new AI-CDSS for community-dwelling patients with CLD. The goal of this AI-CDSS is to predict the probability that patients would benefit from 5 frailty- and depression-focused interventions (pulmonary rehabilitation, physical therapy, fall-risk assessment, nutrition consultation, and depression consultation). In this study, pulmonologists will review the AI-CDSS's predictions and have the option to recommend referrals for their patients. If a referral is recommended, the study team will contact the patient to discuss the referral and start the referral process. All participants will then complete a semi-structured interview and feedback survey asking their opinions about the AI-CDSS and the study referral process.

title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
desc: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
desc: Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models. Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO). Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios. Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation. Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.

title: STREAM: Sequential Transformer for Risk Estimation from Asynchronous Medical Events for Dynamic Postoperative AKI Prediction
desc: Postoperative acute kidney injury (PO-AKI) risk estimates evolve as clinical information accumulates, yet many electronic health record (EHR) models use static or fixed-window representations. We developed STREAM, a perioperative event-stream Transformer that represents irregular EHR data as chronological clinical events and supports surgery-index prediction at surgery completion and event-by-event postoperative AKI prediction. In a retrospective cohort of 167,078 noncardiac surgical episodes, STREAM achieved surgery-index AUROC/AUPRC of 0.942/0.771, the Time-series Transformer 0.933/0.729, and GRU-D 0.926/0.695. Postoperative macro-AUPRC across 6-hour evaluation intervals was 0.589, 0.525, and 0.547, respectively. STREAM showed more consistent calibration across postoperative time points than the comparators. Event-arrival attribution and within-window permutation analysis enabled event-level interpretation of how newly arrived information and fine-grained event ordering shaped evolving risk estimates. These findings support event-stream modeling as an interpretable framework for dynamic, temporally resolved prediction from longitudinal EHR data as well as a potential risk-estimation component for future perioperative digital twins.

title: XenoType: Decoding cellular identity in breast cancer histology through molecular supervision
desc: Characterizing the cellular composition of the tumor microenvironment from histological images is fundamental to understanding cancer biology and informing treatment decisions. Deep learning has enabled automated nuclear detection and classification from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images, yet cell classifiers remain largely confined to broad morphological categories owing to a reliance on manual annotations. Recent efforts have used spatial molecular measurements to supervise histological classification, but these approaches often require separate tissue sections or produce altered H&E staining, and the resulting cell-type annotations depend on subjective choices such as marker selection and clustering parameters. Here we develop XenoType, a framework that classifies cells into seven molecularly informed categories directly from routine histology, trained using paired same-section Xenium spatial transcriptomics. Cell-type annotations are reconciled from four single-cell RNA-sequencing references, reducing dependence on marker choices. Across eight held-out breast tissue sections, XenoType outperformed commonly used CellViT++ retrained on the same molecular annotations under both four-class (macro-F1: 0.703 vs. 0.569) and seven-class (macro-F1: 0.571 vs. 0.403) taxonomies, with the largest gains for myoepithelial (F1: 0.175 to 0.572) and endothelial cells (F1: 0.395 to 0.682). Molecular measurements are required only during training; at inference, XenoType uses the H&E image alone. Model-reference agreement increased consistently with annotation confidence, and XenoType generalized to an independently profiled breast tissue section from a different spatial transcriptomics platform, supporting scalable cell-type mapping from routine histology without per-specimen molecular profiling.
